I ran the committed CLI entry point in-process for all 65,536 documented inputs on Python 3.11.13 and compared stdout with `n.to_bytes(2, "big", signed=False).hex()` plus a newline. The sweep found **32,768 exact matches and 32,768 exceptions**. Separate `python3 -I -B channel.py N` subprocesses confirmed the boundary behavior.

| Channel | Expected stdout | Observed stdout | Exit |
|---:|---|---|---:|
| `260` | `0104` | `0104` | `0` |
| `32767` | `7fff` | `7fff` | `0` |
| `32768` | `8000` | empty | `1` |
| `65535` | `ffff` | empty | `1` |

The documented `python3 -B -m unittest -v` check **passed**. Its one test asserts output for `0` and `260`. CI is **unverified** because the checkout has no configured remote or committed CI workflow. I left the checkout untouched. [test_channel.py](test_channel.py:7)

sessions.subject: 0e9b628d1b57db479922848d809301aa3e41338d
sessions.response:
Make `amount_minor` the canonical GBP minor-unit field. During the transition, collectors should write both `amount_minor` and `total_pence` with the same value. Remove `total_pence` from new records only after every billing version an operator can roll back to can read `amount_minor` on its own.

The [README](README.md:3) makes the shared log the system of record and allows either service to roll back one version without warning. I verified that current billing totals a mixed log containing old and dual-field records, but raises `KeyError` as soon as it encounters a record with only `amount_minor`. Rolling back the collector leaves any records it already appended in the log.

### Implementation and rollout

1. **Release compatible billing.** Update `billing.total` to read old, dual-field, and renamed-only records and count each line once. Use `amount_minor` when present, including when it is zero. Keep support for `total_pence` on historical records. I recommend rejecting a dual-field record with conflicting values so billing surfaces the discrepancy instead of silently choosing a total.
2. **Release the dual-writing collector.** Update `collector.append` to write the same GBP pence value under both keys in one JSON object per line. Keep the existing `append(stream, pence)` interface. This lets collectors and billing deploy and roll back independently while legacy billing remains eligible for rollback.
3. **Verify the rollback floor, then switch to renamed-only writes.** Confirm from release and deployment records that every active billing instance and its actual one-version rollback artifact can read renamed-only records. This may require a second compatible billing release. Until that gate passes, keep dual-writing. Once it passes, release the collector that writes only `amount_minor`. Keep historical billing read support and leave the shared log intact. Confirm with the release owner which artifacts operators can actually restore.

### Rollout checks

| Acceptance criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Billing reads the full log across the transition | Feed `billing.total` old-only `3`, dual-field `5`, renamed-only `7`, and renamed-only `0`. Expect `15`. Verify a conflicting dual-field record fails explicitly. |
| Each collector release writes the intended record | Parse the actual output of `collector.append` for `0` and `5`. Expect one JSON line per call, with identical values under both keys during the bridge and only `amount_minor` after cutover. |
| Either service can roll back during the bridge | Replay a log with old and dual-field records through current and previous billing artifacts. Roll the collector back, append an old-format record, and verify both billing artifacts still produce the expected total. |
| Cutover is safe after renamed-only records persist | In staging, write renamed-only records with the candidate collector, then replay that same log with the billing rollback artifact. Roll back the collector, append again, and verify both supported billing artifacts still total the full log. Use these results and the production version inventory as the cutover gate. |

Run the repository suite with `python3 -B -m unittest -v`. The existing round-trip test passed at clean revision `0e9b628d1b57db479922848d809301aa3e41338d`. The rollout checks above are planned checks. The checkout was left unchanged.

sessions.subject: 0e9b628d1b57db479922848d809301aa3e41338d
sessions.response:
Rename the persisted GBP minor-unit field from `total_pence` to `amount_minor`. Deploy compatible billing readers first, then switch collectors once both the live billing version and its one-version rollback target can read either field. The first `amount_minor`-only append is the point after which legacy billing can no longer read the shared log.

The checkout was clean at `0e9b628d1b57db479922848d809301aa3e41338d` and was left unchanged. The existing unit test passed on Python 3.11.13. A read-only check also confirmed that current billing raises `KeyError` when a mixed log reaches an `amount_minor`-only record. [README.md](README.md) · [billing.py](billing.py)

## Implementation and deployment

1. **Release a compatible billing reader.** Update `billing.total` to read `amount_minor` when present and fall back to `total_pence`. Sum one amount per line, preserve zero values, and keep support for historical records for as long as the log retains them. Keep collectors on the existing format during this release. [billing.py](billing.py)
2. **Establish the billing rollback floor.** With ordinary previous-release rollback, deploy a second compatible billing release so the first compatible release becomes the rollback target. Operations should verify the actual live and rollback artifacts across every billing deployment that reads the shared log. Hold the collector release until both artifacts pass the replay check below.
3. **Switch the collector.** Update `collector.append` to emit `{"amount_minor": pence}` as one JSON object per line. Keep the GBP units and the `append(stream, pence)` interface. Canary the writer and watch billing for parse errors, interrupted processing, or total discrepancies before expanding. If the canary fails, rolling back the collector restores legacy writes for future appends. Billing still needs a compatible version because new-format records already in the log remain there. [collector.py](collector.py)

A temporary dual-write release could let collectors ship earlier by writing both keys with the same value. It would add an intermediate format and still require the same billing rollback gate before removing `total_pence`. Use the reader-first sequence to keep the migration to the two intended formats and avoid rewriting the system of record.

## Rollout checks

| Check | Passing result |
| --- | --- |
| Collector output through `append` | Appending `5` produces exactly one newline-terminated JSON record with `{"amount_minor": 5}`. |
| Historical and mixed records through `total` | Legacy `3` totals `3`, new-format `5` totals `5`, and a mix of legacy `3`, new-format `5`, and new-format `0` totals `8` in either order. A record missing both keys raises an error. |
| Independent rollback on a disposable log | Append legacy `3` and new-format `5`. Run both the live and rollback billing artifacts against that same log and verify each returns `8`. Roll back the collector, append legacy `2`, then verify both billing artifacts return `10` on the same log. |
| Production gate and canary | Operations confirms the billing rollback target is compatible before the first new-format append. During the canary, billing continues processing and its totals match independently summed amounts for the same records. |

Add the focused cases to the existing suite and run `python3 -B -m unittest discover -v`. The checkout contains no deployment configuration, so the release team needs access to the deployed artifacts and rollback controls to verify the production gate. [test_ledger.py](test_ledger.py)

**No. The branch suppresses repeated calls after an acknowledged append, but a lost acknowledgement still causes duplicate delivery.**

**[P1] Make enqueue idempotent by record ID.** The queue can persist a record and then lose its acknowledgement. When that happens, `queue.append(record)` raises before `sent.add(...)` runs. The caller retries, finds the ID absent from `sent`, and appends the same record again. I reproduced this with the supplied Python interpreter. After the timeout, the queue contained `['17']` and `sent` was empty. After the retry, the queue contained `['17', '17']`. [outbox.py](outbox.py:4) · [README.md](README.md:3)

Enforce uniqueness by record ID atomically with the durable append. Moving `sent.add(...)` before the append would suppress retries even when the first append fails before storing the record. Add a regression test that stores the record, raises a timeout, retries, and asserts that exactly one entry exists. The branch’s repeated-success test passed. [test_outbox.py](test_outbox.py:7)
